title: “ADULTERY IN THE HEART”: Can Sexual Sin Happen Without Physical Contact?
paragraphs: “ADULTERY IN THE HEART”: Can Sexual Sin Happen Without Physical Contact?
Jesus said adultery can happen where nobody else can see it. But what exactly did He mean—and have we misunderstood one of His most uncomfortable warnings?
Nobody touched anybody.
No hotel room.
No secret meeting.
No physical affair.
No incriminating photograph.
Maybe nobody else on earth even knows.
And yet Jesus speaks words so penetrating that they leave nowhere for the human heart to hide.
“Adultery.”
That word usually makes us imagine bodies crossing a forbidden boundary.
Jesus takes us somewhere earlier.
Into the place before the bedroom.
Before the message.
Before the meeting.
Before the physical betrayal.
Into the heart.
And perhaps that is what makes Matthew 5:27–28 so uncomfortable.
Because you can hide a browser history.
You can delete a conversation.
You can close an app.
You can maintain a respectable reputation.
You can sit in church with your Bible open.
But you cannot delete anything from the eyes of Christ.
He sees the heart.
And what He says next is devastating.
Matthew records Jesus saying:
“Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη· Οὐ μοιχεύσεις.”
Ēkousate hoti errethē: Ou moicheuseis.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’”
Then Jesus continues:
“ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman toward desiring her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:27–28.
Read those words again slowly.
Not because Jesus is trying to make ordinary human existence impossible.
Not because noticing that another human being is physically attractive automatically makes someone an adulterer.
Not because temptation itself is identical to surrender.
The wording matters.
Jesus speaks of the one who is “looking”—βλέπων, blepōn—and then gives the direction or purpose of that look:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν.
Pros to epithymēsai autēn.
Toward desiring her.
The verb ἐπιθυμέω, epithymeō, can describe desire, longing, or coveting depending on context. Here the context is adultery.
Jesus is exposing the deliberate cultivation of sexual desire toward someone who is not rightfully yours.
That distinction matters.
There is a difference between seeing and staring.
Between noticing and nourishing.
Between temptation arriving at your door and inviting it inside.
Between an unwanted thought flashing through the mind and choosing to replay the fantasy because you enjoy what it gives you.
You may not control every temptation that appears.
But what do you do with it when it arrives?
That is where this passage becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes sexual sin does not begin when two bodies touch.
Sometimes it begins when the heart whispers:
Stay.
Look again.
Imagine more.
Nobody will know.
And instead of fleeing, we feed it.
That second look becomes a third.
That image becomes another.
That profile becomes a ritual.
That conversation becomes increasingly suggestive.
That private fantasy becomes somewhere we repeatedly visit.
Nothing physical has happened.
Yet something is happening.
Jesus refuses to let outward respectability become camouflage for inward rebellion.
That is the scandal of His words.
A person can appear faithful while privately feeding unfaithfulness.
A husband can technically never touch another woman while repeatedly undressing women in his imagination.
A wife can never physically enter another man's bed while secretly nurturing erotic or romantic fantasies about someone else.
A single believer can say, “But I'm not married, so technically I can't cheat on anyone,” while still training the heart to consume people sexually rather than honor them as image-bearers of God.
Pornography can make this deception especially easy.
Nobody touched you.
You touched nobody.
So the conscience tries to negotiate.
“At least I didn't actually do anything.”
But Jesus destroys the loophole.
The Kingdom of God is not merely concerned with where your body has been.
Christ cares about what your heart is becoming.
That is why this teaching is so much bigger than a prohibition against adultery.
Jesus is revealing something about holiness itself.
God does not merely want restrained hands.
He wants transformed hearts.
And suddenly the question changes.
It is no longer only:
“Did I sleep with someone?”
It becomes:
“What am I teaching my heart to desire?”
What do you repeatedly watch when nobody is around?
Whose body have you turned into material for private fantasy?
Which conversations do you keep returning to because they give you an emotional or sexual thrill you know you should not be feeding?
What would embarrass you if your spouse saw it?
What would you immediately close if Jesus physically walked into the room?
And perhaps the most piercing question of all:
Why are we imagining that He wasn't already there?
There is a strange insanity to secret sin.
We hide from people...
while sinning before the God from whom nothing is hidden.
We delete evidence...
while standing before the One who searches hearts.
We become terrified that a husband, wife, parent, pastor, friend, or church member might discover what God already sees perfectly.
Yet this is where this article could become crushing if we stopped too soon.
Because Matthew 5 was never given so that respectable sinners could point fingers at less respectable sinners.
Jesus takes the commandment and drives it through our carefully constructed categories until every self-righteous person has a problem.
Maybe you never committed physical adultery.
But have you ever deliberately cherished lust?
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus knows.
And if that makes you uncomfortable...
good.
But don't run from Him.
Because the One exposing the darkness is also the One who came to rescue sinners from it.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not the announcement that sexually spotless people may approach Jesus.
Christianity is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The sexually broken.
The porn-addicted.
The adulterer.
The fantasizer.
The ashamed.
The person who promised God, “Never again,” and then fell again.
The person whose marriage has been wounded.
The person carrying memories they desperately wish they could erase.
The person who has learned how to worship publicly while collapsing privately.
Jesus did not come because humanity was clean.
He came because we weren't.
And grace does not mean Jesus suddenly calls darkness light.
Grace means our darkness does not have the final word when we come to Christ in repentance and faith.
This is where many people misunderstand the Gospel.
They imagine only two possibilities.
Either minimize the sin so they don't have to feel ashamed...
or admit the sin and believe they are permanently ruined.
Jesus offers neither.
He does not minimize sin.
And He does not tell the repentant sinner that redemption is impossible.
He exposes.
He calls us to repentance.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He transforms.
He teaches us to fight what once enslaved us.
That is why biblical conviction and condemnation are not identical experiences.
Conviction brings the darkness into the light so that we can turn toward Christ.
Hopeless shame whispers:
“Hide from God.”
The Gospel says:
“Come into the light.”
Sin says:
“Keep pretending.”
Jesus says:
“Follow Me.”
Your sexual history may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to write the final chapter of your life.
Your worst night is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
Your secret browser history is not stronger than the cross.
Your affair is not stronger than the cross.
Your fantasies are not stronger than the cross.
Your shame is not stronger than the cross.
But grace is not permission to keep feeding what nailed Christ to that cross.
Grace teaches us to come out of hiding.
And Jesus' next words in Matthew 5 show just how seriously He wants His disciples to treat sin.
He speaks of tearing out the right eye and cutting off the right hand if they cause someone to stumble.
Jesus is using deliberately shocking language to communicate the radical seriousness with which sin must be confronted.
He is not giving Christians permission to mutilate their bodies.
Removing an eye would not remove lust from the heart anyway.
The problem Jesus has just identified is deeper.
The heart needs transformation.
But sometimes genuine repentance requires ruthless practical changes.
Delete the account.
Block the website.
End the flirtation.
Stop privately messaging the person.
Move the phone out of the bedroom.
Stop calling pornography “stress relief.”
Stop calling emotional infidelity “just friendship.”
Stop deliberately placing yourself where you know your resistance repeatedly collapses.
Tell a mature, trustworthy believer that you need accountability.
If your marriage has been wounded, pursue truth, repentance, wise pastoral care, and where appropriate professional counseling.
Stop protecting the darkness that is destroying you.
Because you cannot simultaneously starve a sin and keep feeding it.
And please hear this carefully:
The goal is not merely behavior modification.
You can install every filter available and still have a heart desperately searching for another idol.
The deepest question is not merely, “How do I stop looking?”
It is:
“What am I looking for when I look?”
Comfort?
Escape?
Power?
Validation?
Novelty?
Control?
Intimacy?
A momentary anesthesia for loneliness?
Sexual sin often promises something much larger than sex.
It whispers that it can soothe pain.
Make you feel wanted.
Make you forget.
Give you control.
Help you escape.
Then it takes far more than it promised to cost.
It offers pleasure without covenant.
Intimacy without vulnerability.
Bodies without souls.
Desire without responsibility.
Escape without healing.
And afterward?
The screen goes dark.
The fantasy ends.
The conversation stops.
And somehow the emptiness remains.
Because pornography cannot love you.
Fantasy cannot know you.
Lust cannot heal you.
And another human body cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
Only Jesus can meet the deepest hunger of the human soul.
That does not mean sexual desire itself is evil.
God created human sexuality.
Within His design it is not dirty, embarrassing, or inherently sinful.
The problem is not that human beings can experience desire.
The problem is what sin does with desire.
It takes a gift and detaches it from God's boundaries.
It takes a person made in God's image and turns that person into an object for consumption.
Lust asks:
“What can this person's body give me?”
Love asks:
“How can I honor this person before God?”
Lust consumes.
Love seeks another's good.
Lust reduces.
Love recognizes dignity.
Lust wants the body while ignoring the soul.
Christ calls us to see the whole person.
And that is why victory cannot simply mean becoming better at looking away.
Christ wants to teach us how to see differently.
To see women as daughters, sisters, neighbors, and image-bearers—not objects.
To see men as sons, brothers, neighbors, and image-bearers—not fantasies.
To see our spouses not as possessions but as people entrusted to our faithful love.
To see our own bodies not as instruments for endless appetite but as belonging to God.
Maybe this article found you after another failure.
Maybe five minutes ago you were looking at something you shouldn't.
Maybe nobody knows about the conversations.
Maybe you have carried a secret for years.
Maybe you're reading this while lying beside someone who believes your heart belongs completely to them.
And something inside you is breaking.
Do not waste that moment.
Don't turn conviction into another promise you make emotionally tonight and forget tomorrow morning.
Bring the truth into the light.
Repentance is more than feeling terrible.
It is turning.
It is agreeing with God about the sin and turning toward Christ.
You may need to confess.
You may need accountability.
You may need to make changes that feel drastic.
You may need to surrender access to something you have protected for years.
But do not confuse losing access to your chains with losing freedom.
The chain was never freedom.
Jesus is.
And if you have already fallen sexually, hear the Gospel before shame distorts everything you just read.
Jesus did not die only for the sins you consider respectable.
The cross was built for guilty people.
First John 1:9 says that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
First Corinthians 6 describes people whose former lives included serious sexual sin, then gives one of the most beautiful turns in Scripture:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because they became their own saviors.
They were washed.
Sanctified.
Justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace rewriting what the scandal thought would be the ending.
Maybe that is your word today.
Were.
You were enslaved.
You were hiding.
You were living two lives.
You were feeding something that was slowly consuming you.
But Jesus Christ is still saving sinners.
And sanctification means your present struggle does not have to become your permanent identity.
You may have to fight repeatedly.
Fight.
You may need someone beside you.
Tell them.
You may stumble and need to repent again.
Run back to Christ.
Do not turn repeated temptation into permission for surrender.
And do not turn a fall into an excuse to stay on the ground.
Get up.
Come into the light.
Follow Jesus again.
Somebody reading this has spent years believing, “If people knew what goes through my mind, they would never look at me the same way.”
Perhaps.
People are imperfect.
But Jesus already knows.
Every thought.
Every search.
Every fantasy.
Every failure.
Every rationalization.
Every relapse.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Believe.
Come.
Not because the sin doesn't matter.
Because the Savior is greater.
No graphic confession.
No performance.
Just honesty.
Someone reading the comments may realize for the first time that they are not the only Christian fighting a war nobody else can see.
And perhaps your honesty will help another person choose the light tonight.
Not because saving a post changes a heart.
Only God can do that.
Come back when the screen starts whispering.
Come back when loneliness starts negotiating.
Come back when your mind tells you, “Just once.”
Then remember:
Jesus wants more for you than momentary escape.
You do not have to know who they are.
You probably won't.
That is the point.
Some of the fiercest spiritual battles happen behind completely ordinary profile pictures.
Send it privately to a struggling believer.
Send it to the friend who keeps returning to pornography and believes change is impossible.
Let truth travel farther than shame.
Stay close to the Word.
Stay close to believers who will tell you the truth.
Stay close to Christ.
Christian giving must not be manipulated.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving is to come from what a person has purposed in the heart—not reluctantly or under compulsion.
He will not.
You cannot.
The favor we desperately need is found in Jesus Christ, not in a transaction.
If you want to support that mission voluntarily and help us reach farther:
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help.
Because somewhere tonight there is a person hiding behind a locked screen.
A spouse wondering why secrecy has entered the marriage.
A teenager learning desire from pornography before learning covenant from Scripture.
A believer convinced that because the sin happened only in the imagination, God does not care.
Another believer convinced that because God does care, God could never want them again.
Both need the truth.
Jesus takes hidden sin more seriously than we sometimes want Him to.
And Jesus receives repentant sinners more graciously than shame wants us to believe.
That is the tension of the Gospel.
Sin is worse than our excuses say.
Grace is greater than our despair says.
The answer to “Can sexual sin happen without physical contact?” is therefore yes: Jesus explicitly teaches that adultery can be committed in the heart when lust is deliberately cultivated.
But His teaching is not an invitation to obsessive terror over every involuntary thought or every moment of noticing another person's attractiveness.
It is a summons to stop making peace with cherished lust.
Stop feeding it.
Stop protecting it.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Bring it to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Cut off what feeds it.
Receive His mercy.
Walk in the light.
And begin learning to see human beings again—not as bodies to consume, but as souls bearing the image of God.
Maybe nobody else knows your scandal.
Jesus does.
And strangely...
that may be the best news you have heard all day.
Because the One who knows the whole story is the very One who went to the cross to save sinners.
The secret you are terrified of bringing into Christ's light may be the very place where grace begins rewriting your story.
